description: Hi. I love figuring out how things work, and then trying to build them myself. Robotics is my favourite: there’s something exciting about writing a few lines of code and watching a machine move because of it. I enjoy building things with my hands, from small models to circuits, and I like coding just as much, whether it’s a game, a website or a robot’s brain. Space Traveller started the same way, as an idea I wanted to see come to life.
summary:
Space Traveller is a free browser game for students aged 8–12 that turns real mission trade-offs into hands-on play. Players choose one of the eight planets and pack their spacecraft with a limited number of modules: solar panels, nuclear power, an air maker, a water maker, a greenhouse, a radiation shield or supplies. They then pilot it along a 3D space path to their destination, where space rocks can damage their cargo. After landing, they walk their astronaut around the outpost to explore, repair or rest, and keep the crew’s air, water, food and health going for 10 days.

The game addresses the challenge by making students live with the results of their engineering choices. Solar power fails at Neptune, dust storms block it on Mars, and the crew needs a shield against radiation storms on Mercury. A clear report card explains why a mission succeeded or failed and adds a fact from a real NASA mission.

This matters because space engineering is about balancing limited power, mass and life support. Space Traveller lets students fail safely and learn why, which builds the problem-solving skills future explorers need.
details:
Project details: Space Traveller

What it does and how it works

Space Traveller is a free browser game for students aged 10–14. Each mission has five steps:

  1. Choose a planet. Players pick one of the eight planets. Each has real differences in sunlight, radiation, cold and water. Earth is a training level.
  2. Pack the ship. Players choose 4–5 modules: solar panels, nuclear power, an air maker, a water maker, a greenhouse, a radiation shield or a supply crate. The space is limited, so every choice is a trade-off. A mission check warns about problems, but players can still launch and learn from mistakes.
  3. Launch and fly. After a countdown, liftoff and stage separation, players steer the ship along a curving 3D space path with the arrow keys, or with on-screen buttons on phones. They collect science and dodge space rocks that damage their cargo. Banners show when they cross other planets’ orbits, and a minimap shows the curves ahead.
  4. Run the outpost. Players walk their astronaut around the base with W A S D. Each day they choose to explore for science, fix a broken module or rest the crew. They must keep air, water, food and health up for 10 days, while handling dust storms, radiation storms, breakdowns and cold snaps.
  5. Read the report card. It shows stars and badges, explains why the mission succeeded or failed, and shares a real fact from a NASA mission. Players earn SpaceCoins to spend on ship upgrades in the Hangar.

Benefits

  • It turns abstract engineering trade-offs into choices students can see and feel. Solar panels fail at Neptune, dust storms cut solar power on Mars, and skipping the shield on Mercury hurts the crew.
  • Students learn by failing safely and seeing exactly why things went wrong.
  • It’s simple to play: four bars, three daily jobs and one mission takes about 5–10 minutes. That fits a classroom lesson.
  • It’s free, needs no account, collects no personal data, works offline and runs on computers, tablets and phones.

Intended impact

We want young students to understand that space missions depend on balancing power, mass, life support and safety. We hope it builds problem-solving skills and curiosity about science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM) careers. Teachers can use it to start class discussions, such as “Why does Neptune need nuclear power?” Every planet’s facts come from real NASA missions, including MOXIE, MESSENGER, Juno, Cassini, Voyager 2 and CHAPEA.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no game engine or frameworks.
  • Graphics: HTML5 Canvas. The planets, 3D space path, launch animation, outpost and astronaut are all drawn in code.
  • Installable app: a web app manifest and a service worker, so it can be installed and played offline.
  • Phone features: touch controls, landscape mode and vibration feedback (including on iPhone).
  • Hosting: GitHub and GitHub Pages.
  • Testing: Playwright for automatic play-testing on different screen sizes, and for balancing the difficulty of each planet.
  • Video: FFmpeg to make the demo video.
  • AI help: we used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and test the code.
  • Hardware: laptops and phones for testing. No special hardware is needed to play.

Creativity and design

The game combines three kinds of play in one mission: planning (packing), action (piloting) and management (running the outpost). Each planet changes the rules, so players have to think differently each time. We kept the controls and screens simple so younger students can focus on the science and their decisions.
